newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU eyes new "Millennium Round" of trade talks.
newsitem.headline: EU eyes new "Millennium Round" of trade talks.

text.p: This week's inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation should pave the way for an ambitious new round of global trade talks by the end of the century, the European Union said on Monday.

European Commission vice-president Sir Leon Brittan said the challenge at Singapore was not only to make progress in pressing areas such as information technology and telecommunications, but also to ensure the WTO fixed its sights firmly on the future.

"This week's decisions should make it possible for us to launch in due course the further broad-based round of talks, which could properly be called the Millennium Round, that I personally believe can start by the end of the century," Brittan told the opening session of the week-long ministerial talks.
"That is not something to decide today. But in all our decisions here in Singapore, we should prepare ourselves so that WTO is ready to take up that challenge in the years ahead," he added.

There is little enthusiasm among world trade officials for new multilateral trade negotiations so soon after the completion in 1994 of the sweeping package of liberalisation measures negotiated under the Uruguay Round of talks.

Developing countries in particular argue that they need more time to adjust their economies to the market-opening demands made of them under the Uruguay Round and are reluctant to agree to put "new issues" such as investment and competition on the WTO's agenda for future work.
Brittan, acknowledging those concerns, said the European Commission, the Brussels-based executive of the European Union, was not looking for immediate long-term commitments.
"A work programme does not prejudge any possible future decision to move to negotiations. This will be for us all to take freely, later," he said.

On the immediate agenda facing ministers, Brittan said the Singapore talks would be judged a failure if it did not make progress toward agreements to free up world trade in telecommunications and information technology.

"I should not have to say that we all have to make a further effort. But we do. If we do not make substantial progress on both issues this week, with new offers tabled, then our meeting will not be the big success we all want," he said.
Brittan expressed confidence that a compromise could be found on the controversial issue of the link between free trade and labour standards.
Developing countries are worried that demands for core standards in areas such as child labour and the right to form trade unions amount to thinly veiled protectionism.
But Brittan said apparently domestic issues were now a legitimate concern for the WTO because voters in developed countries were demanding action.
"Only when the WTO is seen to meet the aspirations of our constituents can we be sure of keeping the way open for continued trade liberalisation'" he said.

He said the European Union, which is itself deeply divided on whether to link trade and workers' rights, shared the desire to ensure that respect for labour standards should not be a cloak for protectionism.
"I think we have the makings of an understanding on that issue, which I hope will provide the basis for some WTO continuity beyond Singapore in this discussion," he said.
